ML Coding · Unsupervised Learning · Class 04

Gaussian Mixture Models

Every algorithm so far forced a hard choice: exactly one cluster, no exceptions. GMM asks a more honest question — how well does each of K bell-curves explain this exact point — and keeps the answer as a genuine probability, not a guess.

01 · nutshell revision

Everything so far, in one page

K-Means / K-Means++

Pick K centroids, assign every point to its nearest one, move each centroid to the mean of its group, repeat. K-Means++ only changes how the starting centroids are chosen (farther-apart points get priority) — the assignment rule stays "nearest centroid wins."

Hierarchical (Agglomerative)

No centroids, no K upfront. Start with every point as its own cluster, repeatedly merge the two closest clusters (Single/Complete/Average/Ward define "closest"), until one giant cluster remains. K is chosen afterward by cutting the resulting dendrogram.

Hierarchical (Divisive)

The mirror image: start with all points in ONE cluster, repeatedly split the highest-SSE cluster into two (via bisecting K-Means), until every point is its own cluster (or you stop early at your desired K).

AlgorithmOne-line analogy
K-Means"Which neighbourhood centre is closest to this person?"
K-Means++"Before starting, let's intelligently choose neighbourhood centres that are spread apart."
Agglomerative Hierarchical"Everyone starts alone. Keep merging nearby groups."
Divisive Hierarchical"Everyone starts together. Keep splitting groups."
What every one of these algorithms has in common, without exception: every customer is assigned to exactly one cluster, with total certainty. There is no "maybe," no partial membership, no in-between. Today, we break that assumption.
02 · naming what we've been doing

Hard clustering — what we've actually been doing this whole time

Everything in Classes 01-03 falls under one umbrella, and it has a name: hard clustering.

xi → exactly ONE cluster

Example: Customer A → Cluster 1. Full stop. No ambiguity, no partial credit.

AlgorithmHow it assigns membership
K-Means / K-Means++Nearest centroid wins — 100% or 0%, nothing between
Hierarchical (either direction)Once the dendrogram is cut at a chosen K, every point falls on exactly one side of every cut — 100% or 0%
Hard clustering isn't wrong — it's simply making an assumption: that every real-world customer, transaction, or data point truly, unambiguously belongs to exactly one group. Section 03 asks: is that assumption always true?
03 · but reality can be fuzzy

Soft clustering — when "exactly one cluster" isn't honest

Suppose a customer spends like a premium customer, but visits like a regular customer, and their purchase frequency sits right between the two groups. Should we confidently say "100% Cluster 1"? Maybe not.

WHAT YOU SEE: the same customer base, viewed two ways. LEFT (hard): a hard boundary line forces every point, including the ambiguous "Customer X," onto exactly one side. RIGHT (soft): Customer X keeps a genuine degree of membership in both groups — say 70% Cluster 1, 30% Cluster 2 — instead of being forced into a confident lie.

Soft clustering, defined

A point can have a degree of membership in multiple clusters simultaneously, instead of being forced into exactly one. Example: Cluster 1 = 0.70, Cluster 2 = 0.25, Cluster 3 = 0.05 — all three memberships coexist, and they add up to 1.

Real industry scenarios where this genuinely matters

Industry scenarioWhy "exactly one cluster" fails hereWhat soft clustering gives you
Customer segmentation (marketing)A customer transitioning from "Discount Hunter" to "Premium" doesn't flip overnight — they're genuinely in between for monthsTarget them with a BLEND of both campaigns, weighted by their actual membership
Document / topic modelingA news article about "the economics of climate policy" is genuinely about BOTH economics AND environment — forcing one topic loses informationTag the article with both topics, weighted by relevance
Medical diagnosis supportA patient's symptoms may partially overlap two conditions — a hard label hides real diagnostic uncertainty from the doctorSurface the actual uncertainty (60% condition A, 40% condition B) instead of hiding it
Genetics / population studiesAn individual's ancestry is often genuinely a mix of populations, not purely oneReport actual mixture proportions instead of a forced single label
Who benefits, concretely: anyone making a decision FROM the cluster label benefits from knowing the real confidence behind it. A marketing team that sends 100% of the "in-between" customers a single hard-coded campaign wastes budget on the ~30% who don't fit; a team that knows the true 70/30 split can blend messaging, or simply flag genuinely ambiguous customers for a human to review instead of guessing.
Today's algorithm: Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) — a clustering algorithm built from the ground up to output exactly this kind of soft, probabilistic membership, instead of a single hard label.
StageIdea
K-MeansNearest centre
HierarchicalMerge / Split
GMMProbabilistic membership
04 · one prerequisite first

Before GMM: what is a Gaussian?

GMM literally stands for Gaussian Mixture Model. Before understanding the model, we need to properly understand the Gaussian (Normal) distribution it's built from — mean, variance, std dev, and the PDF formula itself, all from first principles.

05 · the foundational object

The Probability Density Function (PDF) — what it actually is

Suppose 7 customers spend these amounts: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16. These values cluster around roughly 13. A Gaussian PDF is simply a smooth curve that describes how likely different spending values are, based on where the data is concentrated.

WHAT YOU SEE: the 7 actual data points (gold dots) sitting on the x-axis, and the smooth bell curve that best describes their spread. NOTICE: the curve peaks exactly at the mean (13.0) and tapers off symmetrically — values near 13 are common, values far from 13 are rare.

Probability vs. Likelihood — the distinction that trips everyone up

ProbabilityLikelihood
What it measuresHow likely a RANGE of outcomes isHow well ONE specific point fits the curve
Computed asAREA under the curve, over a rangeThe HEIGHT of the curve at one point (the PDF value)
Always between 0 and 1?Yes, alwaysNo — a PDF value can exceed 1 (it's a density, not a probability)
WHAT YOU SEE, LEFT: the likelihood at x=171 is simply the curve's HEIGHT there (0.0352 in this example) — a single number describing how well that one point fits, NOT a probability. RIGHT: the probability P(X ≤ 171) is the shaded AREA under the curve up to that point (0.540) — this one genuinely IS a probability, between 0 and 1.
Why this distinction matters for everything that follows: when GMM decides "how well does this Gaussian explain this data point," it uses likelihood (the curve's height at that point) — never probability. This is why likelihood values you'll see later in this class can look like "0.176" or even numbers that don't resemble a 0-1 probability at all in higher dimensions.

The PDF formula, for one dimension

$$P(x \mid \mu, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$$

This formula takes a value $x$, and two parameters — $\mu$ (mean) and $\sigma$ (standard deviation) — and returns the height of the curve at that point. That height is the likelihood. Everything about a 1D Gaussian is controlled by just these two numbers.

06 · the two numbers that define everything

Mean, Variance, and Standard Deviation

Mean (μ) — "Where is the centre?"

$$\mu = \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n}{n}$$

For our 7 spending values (10 through 16): $\mu = \frac{10+11+12+13+14+15+16}{7} = \frac{91}{7} = 13.0$.

Variance (σ²) — "How spread out is the data?"

Mean alone doesn't tell us how spread out the data is. Compare two customer groups:

GroupValuesMeanSpread
A9, 10, 11, 12, 1311Very concentrated
B1, 5, 11, 17, 2111Much more spread out
Both groups have the exact same mean (11) — but they look completely different. Variance is what captures that difference.
$$\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \mu)^2$$

Variance measures the average squared distance from the mean. Worked for Group A:

xx − μ(x − μ)²
9−24
10−11
1100
1211
1324
Sum = 10σ² = 10 / 5 = 2.0

Standard Deviation (σ) — variance, back in original units

Variance is in squared units (e.g. "spending² "), which is hard to interpret directly. Standard deviation is just $\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}$ — for Group A, $\sigma = \sqrt{2.0} = 1.41$, back in the same units as spending itself.

Summary: Mean (μ) tells us the position of the Gaussian distribution. Standard deviation (σ) tells us its shape (how wide or narrow). These two numbers are the entire distribution.
07 · isolating one parameter at a time

What happens when we change the MEAN (σ held constant)?

If we change the mean of the distribution, the position of the distribution changes. The shape of the distribution does NOT change.

WHAT YOU SEE: three Gaussians, all with the identical standard deviation (σ=10), but centred at μ=150, 170, and 190. NOTICE: all three curves are IDENTICAL in width and height — they're just shifted left or right along the x-axis. Changing μ is a pure horizontal translation, nothing else.
08 · the other parameter, isolated

What happens when we change the STANDARD DEVIATION (μ held constant)?

When we change the std dev (or variance), the shape of the distribution changes. The position stays exactly where it was.

WHAT YOU SEE: three Gaussians, all centred at the identical mean (μ=170), but with σ=5, 12, and 22. NOTICE: smaller σ (teal) → tall and narrow, tightly concentrated near the mean. Larger σ (coral) → short and wide, spread out over a much bigger range. All three still peak at exactly x=170.
09 · reading the curve correctly

Which points share the SAME likelihood, and which have MORE?

Draw a horizontal line across the curve at any height — every point that line touches shares the exact same likelihood. This single idea becomes the foundation of the concentric circles you'll see in 2D (Section 12).

WHAT YOU SEE: pairs of gold points sitting at equal distances (10 and 20 units) on either side of the mean (μ=170). NOTICE: each pair sits on the SAME horizontal dashed line — meaning they share the exact same likelihood, purely because they're equally far from the mean. The single red point sitting exactly AT the mean has the highest likelihood of any point on the curve.
The rule to carry forward: likelihood depends only on DISTANCE from the mean (scaled by σ), never on direction. Points equidistant from μ — whether above or below it — always tie. The closer to μ, the higher the likelihood; the peak itself, exactly at μ, is the single highest-likelihood point on the whole curve.
10 · beyond one dimension

The 2D (and N-D) Gaussian

Real customer data almost never has just 1 feature — RFM alone has 3 (Recency, Frequency, Monetary). The Gaussian generalizes cleanly to any number of dimensions, using vectors and matrices instead of single numbers.

1D conceptBecomes, in D dimensions
Mean μ (a single number)Mean vector $\vec{\mu} = [\mu_1, \mu_2, ..., \mu_D]$ — one mean per feature
Variance σ² (a single number)Covariance matrix $\Sigma$ (D×D) — variances on the diagonal, PLUS how features move together (covariance) off the diagonal

The 2D covariance matrix, concretely

For 2 features (say, Spend=x and Visits=y):

$$\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix}\sigma_x^2 & \text{Cov}(x,y) \\ \text{Cov}(x,y) & \sigma_y^2\end{bmatrix}_{2\times2}$$

The diagonal ($\sigma_x^2$, $\sigma_y^2$) is just the familiar per-feature variance from Section 06. The off-diagonal term, Cov(x,y), captures something new: do these two features tend to move together? If high spenders also tend to visit more, Cov(x,y) is positive — and the Gaussian's shape TILTS to reflect that relationship (this is exactly the "correlation" slider in the widget below).

The N-Dimensional PDF formula

$$P(\vec{x} \mid \vec{\mu}, \Sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^D |\Sigma|}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\vec{x}-\vec{\mu})^T \Sigma^{-1} (\vec{x}-\vec{\mu})\right)$$
SymbolMeaning
$\vec{x}$a D-dimensional data point (e.g. [Spend, Visits, Recency, ...])
$\vec{\mu}$D×1 mean vector — one mean per feature
$\Sigma$D×D covariance matrix — variances + cross-feature relationships
$|\Sigma|$determinant of the covariance matrix (a single scalar)
$\Sigma^{-1}$the matrix inverse of the covariance matrix
This is EXACTLY the same 1D formula from Section 05, generalized — $(x-\mu)^2/\sigma^2$ has simply become $(\vec{x}-\vec{\mu})^T\Sigma^{-1}(\vec{x}-\vec{\mu})$, and the flat scalar normalizer has become a matrix-determinant version. Same shape of idea, more dimensions.
WHAT YOU SEE, LEFT: the 2D Gaussian as a literal 3D "hill" — height = density. RIGHT: the exact same hill, viewed from directly above — the hill collapses into concentric ELLIPSE rings (not circles, because these two features have some correlation, which tilts the hill). This top view is what you'll see in every 2D GMM plot from now on.

Interactive: build your own 2D Gaussian

Drag the sliders to change each parameter — watch the 3D hill AND the top-view contour rings update together. Rotate the 3D plot by dragging on it.

Play with the sliders above and notice: moving μ1/μ2 slides the hill sideways without changing its shape (Section 07's rule, now in 2D). Changing σ1/σ2 stretches or squeezes the hill along one axis. Changing ρ (correlation) TILTS the ellipse into a diagonal — at ρ=0 you get perfect circles/axis-aligned ellipses; as |ρ| grows toward 1, the ellipse squeezes into a thin diagonal line.
11 · the concentric-rings idea, made concrete

Cutting the hill — where the concentric circles actually come from

Section 09 showed that in 1D, a horizontal line across the curve touches points of equal likelihood. In 2D, the exact same idea becomes a horizontal PLANE slicing through the hill.

WHAT YOU SEE: the same 2D Gaussian hill, sliced by 3 different horizontal planes. Cut near the peak (left) → a small, tight ellipse: only points VERY close to the mean reach this height, so this ring marks HIGH likelihood. Cut in the middle → a bigger ellipse, medium likelihood. Cut near the base (right) → the biggest ellipse, LOW likelihood — practically the whole hill's footprint.
WHAT YOU SEE: all 3 cuts overlaid together — this is exactly the "top view" contour plot from Section 10's widget. NOTICE: every single point sitting ON the same ring shares the identical likelihood — exactly Section 09's 1D rule, just traced out as a 2D ring instead of two mirrored points. The innermost ring is the highest-likelihood region; the outermost is the lowest.
The one sentence to carry into GMM: when GMM later draws an ellipse around a cluster, that ellipse is nothing mysterious — it's just one of these concentric likelihood rings, at whatever height was chosen to draw it (commonly the "2-sigma" ring, containing roughly 95% of that cluster's mass).
12 · finally, the model itself

Gaussian Mixture Model — the setup

The idea behind GMM: fit a Gaussian distribution to each data cluster, and check if a datapoint belongs to that distribution. The more the likelihood of a datapoint belonging to a distribution, the more we can say that datapoint belongs to that cluster. This is nothing but a Gaussian Mixture Model — "mixture" because we're using MORE THAN ONE Gaussian to model our data.

Just like K-Means, you choose K upfront. We decide the number of Gaussians to use, generally based on domain knowledge — exactly the same K-selection problem from Classes 01-03 (elbow, silhouette, dendrogram), just feeding into a different algorithm.

Our dataset for today: 15 customers, K=2

Suppose 15 customers have these spending values: 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 9, 15, 16, 18, 18, 19, 20, 22, 24. We suspect two hidden populations — a lower-spend group and a higher-spend group, of possibly UNEQUAL size. With K=2, we need 3 parameters per Gaussian:

ParameterMeaningQuestion it answers
μ (mu)Mean of this Gaussian"Where is this cluster centred?"
σ² (sigma-squared)Variance of this Gaussian"How spread out is this cluster?"
π (pi)Mixture weight"How common is this cluster overall, as a fraction of the whole population?"

Why do we need π specifically?

Imagine two Gaussian populations: G1 makes up 90% of the population ($\pi_1=0.90$), G2 makes up only 10% ($\pi_2=0.10$). Suppose for one customer, both Gaussians give the SAME density (0.20 each). If we only looked at density, we'd call it a tie. But G1 is much more common in the population overall — so a tie in density should NOT mean a tie in how strongly we believe this point came from each cluster.

G1 (π=0.90)G2 (π=0.10)
Density (raw likelihood)0.200.20
Density × π (weighted)0.180.02
π breaks the tie correctly: "weighted density" = density × π. Since G1 is 9× more common overall, a customer this ambiguous is 9× more likely to have come from G1 — exactly what the weighted numbers (0.18 vs 0.02) show. This weighted quantity — density × π — is called each Gaussian's contribution, and it's the central quantity GMM computes for every point.
One constraint always holds: $\sum_k \pi_k = 1$ — the mixture weights across all K Gaussians must sum to exactly 1, since together they describe the WHOLE population.

Initialization, step by step (1D)

1
Decide K — same as choosing K in K-Means, typically from domain knowledge or by comparing multiple K's later (Section 18).
2
Guess starting values for μ, σ², and π for each of the K Gaussians. These are genuine guesses that will almost certainly be wrong at first — that's expected. The next section (EM) exists specifically to correct them iteratively.
3
Common, principled ways to generate that starting guess (not literally random numbers pulled from nowhere — see the detailed breakdown below).

For our 15-point dataset, here's a genuine (not perfectly-clairvoyant) starting guess:

G1G2
μ8.015.0
Variance (σ²)20.020.0
π0.50.5
Notice this starting guess is deliberately imperfect and the two Gaussians overlap heavily. This is intentional: it lets us see genuinely fractional (not trivial 0-or-1) responsibilities in the E-step below, exactly what happens on real, messy data.

How initialization ACTUALLY happens — μ, σ², π, in detail

"Random" is not quite the right word for how production GMM implementations initialize — each of the three parameter types has its own, more principled default strategy:

ParameterCommon initialization strategyWhy this, not pure random
μ (means)Run K-Means (or K-Means++) first, use its K centroids as the starting meansK-Means centroids are already spread across the data's actual structure — far better than randomly guessed points, and gets EM converging in far fewer iterations
σ² / Σ (variance / covariance)Use the OVERALL dataset's variance/covariance (computed once, from all points, ignoring cluster membership), assigned identically to every Gaussian at startWe don't yet know each cluster's true spread — but the whole dataset's spread is a safe, unbiased starting point that's never wildly wrong in scale
π (mixture weights)Start all equal: $\pi_k = 1/K$ for every GaussianWe have no evidence yet that any cluster is more common than another — equal weights make no unjustified assumption

Specifically for 2D and higher — the covariance matrix at initialization

In 1D, "guess a variance" means picking one number. In D dimensions, we need a full D×D covariance matrix to start from. There are two standard, principled choices:

1
Diagonal, scaled by overall per-feature variance (most common default): compute each feature's variance across the WHOLE dataset independently, put those on the diagonal, and set every off-diagonal (cross-feature) entry to 0 at the start — i.e. assume no correlation between features until the data proves otherwise. This is exactly what we used for our 2D worked example in Section 16: $\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix}500 & 0\\0 & 500\end{bmatrix}$.
2
The full overall covariance matrix (a stronger starting point): compute the ENTIRE dataset's covariance matrix (including cross-feature terms) once, and use that same full matrix as every Gaussian's starting covariance. This captures any global feature correlation from the outset, at the cost of being slightly more expensive to compute upfront.
3
This scales to any D unchanged: for 5D RFM-style data, the same two options apply — a 5×5 diagonal matrix of per-feature variances, or the full 5×5 overall covariance matrix. Nothing about the strategy changes with dimensionality; only the matrix size does.
The one sentence to remember: nothing in GMM's initialization is truly "random" in the sense of arbitrary numbers — means come from K-Means's own sensible starting points, variances/covariances come from the data's own overall spread, and weights start uniform simply because there's no evidence yet to prefer one cluster over another. EM's job (next section) is to correct all three from there.
13 · the engine that fits the model

Why do we need EM (Expectation-Maximization)?

We don't know the true μ, σ², and π for each Gaussian — that's precisely what we're trying to find. So we start with guesses (Section 12), and iteratively improve them using a 2-step loop, repeated until the numbers stop changing.

1
Guess μ, σ², π (Section 12 — already done).
2
E-Step (Expectation): using the CURRENT guesses, estimate the responsibility — how much each Gaussian "owns" each data point.
3
M-Step (Maximization): using those responsibilities, RECALCULATE better μ, σ², π values.
4
Repeat steps 2-3 until the parameters stop changing meaningfully (convergence).
The name, decoded: "Expectation" = the E-step computes an expected (probabilistic) membership for every point. "Maximization" = the M-step re-fits parameters to maximize how well the model explains the data, given those memberships. Together, EM never takes a hard guess — it always works with soft, weighted evidence.
14 · expectation step, in full

E-Step — computing responsibility for EVERY point

"Responsibility" answers one precise question for every single data point: "For THIS customer, how much should each Gaussian take credit for explaining them?" We compute this for all 15 points below — none skipped.

1
Calculate each Gaussian's density at this point (Section 05's PDF formula) — "how well does this Gaussian's shape fit this point, ignoring how common the Gaussian is?"
2
Multiply by π — turns raw density into "contribution" (Section 12) — "how strongly does this component explain the observation, accounting for how common it is overall?"
3
Normalize — divide each Gaussian's contribution by the SUM of all Gaussians' contributions for that point, so the responsibilities for one point always add up to exactly 1.
$$\gamma_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \sigma_k^2)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} \pi_j \, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_j, \sigma_j^2)}$$

$\gamma_{ik}$ (gamma) is the responsibility of Gaussian $k$ for point $i$ — read the whole formula as "this Gaussian's contribution, divided by the total contribution from ALL Gaussians for this exact point."

Totals needed for the M-step

15 · maximization step, in full

M-Step — updating μ, σ², π using the responsibilities

Now that every point has a soft membership (γ) in each Gaussian, we recompute better parameters — each Gaussian's new mean, variance, and weight, using those responsibilities as WEIGHTS in a weighted average.

Updating μ — a responsibility-weighted average

$$\mu_k^{\text{new}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \gamma_{ik}\, x_i}{N_k}$$
Why weighted, not a plain average? A point with γ=0.95 for G1 should pull G1's mean strongly toward it; a point with γ=0.05 should barely move it at all. This formula does exactly that automatically.

Updating σ² — a responsibility-weighted variance

$$(\sigma_k^{\text{new}})^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \gamma_{ik}\,(x_i - \mu_k^{\text{new}})^2}{N_k}$$

Same idea as Section 06's variance formula, but every squared deviation is weighted by how responsible this Gaussian actually is for that point — and it uses the BRAND NEW μ computed just above, not the old one.

This time π genuinely moved — from the uninformed 0.5/0.5 starting guess toward 0.456/0.544, already approaching the true split (7 of 15 = 0.467 in the low-spend group, 8 of 15 = 0.533 in the high-spend group). This is exactly what π is FOR: letting the data tell us one cluster is genuinely more common than the other, instead of assuming they're equal forever.

Repeat — this is the whole loop

These brand-new (μ, σ², π) values become the CURRENT parameters for the next E-step. Recompute all 15 points' responsibilities again with the improved numbers, then M-step again, and so on — until the parameters barely move between iterations (convergence).

WHAT YOU SEE: the two Gaussians evolving over successive EM iterations on our exact 15-point dataset, starting from the overlapping initial guess (μ1=8, μ2=15) shown above. NOTICE: by iteration 6, the curves have fully separated and converged to μ1=5.57, μ2=18.99, π1=0.466, π2=0.534 — landing almost exactly on the true underlying groups {3,4,5,5,6,7,9} and {15,16,18,18,19,20,22,24}, INCLUDING correctly recovering that the two groups are unequal in size, purely from repeating E-step/M-step with no other information.

EM for 2D data — from the very first step

Same dataset intuition, now with 2 features (Spend, Visits). 6 customers: (12,45), (15,50), (10,42), (70,20), (75,25), (68,18) — a low-spend/high-visit group and a high-spend/low-visit group.

Initialization

Same principle as the 1D case: the starting covariance is deliberately wide (500 = std dev ≈ 22) so the two Gaussians genuinely overlap, producing meaningful fractional responsibilities rather than a trivial 0/1 split. This particular starting covariance is the "diagonal, scaled by overall variance" strategy from Section 12 — a 2×2 diagonal matrix, no assumed correlation between Spend and Visits at the start.

Same mechanics as 1D — density is now the 2D PDF from Section 10 (uses the full covariance matrix), but the E-step formula (contribution ÷ total contribution) is IDENTICAL to the 1D case.

M-Step — updating the mean VECTOR

$$\vec{\mu}_k^{\text{new}} = \frac{\sum_i \gamma_{ik}\,\vec{x}_i}{N_k}$$

Exactly Section 15's formula — except now $x_i$ is a 2D vector, so the weighted sum happens independently in each dimension.

N_kΣγ·x (both features)New μ (mean vector)
G12.9305[73.26, 117.87][25.00, 40.22]

M-Step — updating the covariance MATRIX

$$\Sigma_k^{\text{new}} = \frac{\sum_i \gamma_{ik}\,(\vec{x}_i-\vec{\mu}_k^{\text{new}})(\vec{x}_i-\vec{\mu}_k^{\text{new}})^T}{N_k}$$

This is Section 15's variance formula, generalized: instead of squaring a scalar deviation, we take the OUTER PRODUCT of the deviation vector with itself — this single operation produces all 4 entries of the 2×2 matrix (2 variances + 2 identical covariance terms) in one shot.

The pattern to notice across all of Sections 14-16: every formula in 2D is the exact same formula from 1D — sum of γ-weighted values, divided by N_k — just with scalars replaced by vectors/matrices. Nothing conceptually new was introduced going from 1D to 2D.
17 · scaling up further

What about 5D data — or any N dimensions?

Nothing changes. Literally every formula from Sections 14-16 is already written in general form — $x_i$, $\mu_k$, and the outer product in the covariance update all work identically whether you have 2 features or 50.

QuantityShape at D dimensionsFormula (same for every D)
Mean μ_kD × 1 vector$\sum_i \gamma_{ik} x_i / N_k$
Covariance Σ_kD × D matrix$\sum_i \gamma_{ik}(x_i-\mu_k)(x_i-\mu_k)^T / N_k$
Mixture weight π_kscalar$N_k / n$
What DOES change as D grows — the practical concern: the covariance matrix has $D^2$ entries to estimate (technically $D(D+1)/2$ due to symmetry), which grows quadratically. With 5D RFM-style data you need enough points per cluster to reliably estimate a 5×5 covariance matrix (15 unique values); with 50 dimensions, that's 1275 unique values per cluster — you can run out of data to estimate them reliably (the same "curse of dimensionality" concern from Class 02's PCA discussion). In practice, this is why GMM is often applied AFTER dimensionality reduction on very high-D data, not directly on raw 50+ feature datasets.
18 · beyond K=2

What changes for K=3, K=5, or general K clusters?

Nothing structural — every formula already has a general index $k$ running from 1 to K. What changes is purely the AMOUNT of computation, and the shapes you can now represent.

AspectK=2 (what we worked through)General K
Parameters to estimate2 means, 2 covariances, 2 weightsK means, K covariances, K weights
E-step per point2 contributions computed, normalizedK contributions computed, normalized (still always sums to 1)
M-step2 weighted averagesK weighted averages, same formula each
Constraintπ1 + π2 = 1$\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k = 1$
WHAT YOU SEE: the same EM machinery fit to real data with K=2, K=3, and K=5 components. NOTICE: each ellipse is one Gaussian's 2-sigma likelihood ring (Section 11) — as K grows, GMM carves the data into progressively finer, still-elliptical groups. The white × marks are each Gaussian's fitted mean, found by the exact M-step formula from Section 16, just repeated K times per iteration instead of twice.
Choosing K for GMM uses the same toolkit as before — domain knowledge first, then compare candidate K's using metrics (GMM has its own model-selection tools, like BIC/AIC, which we'll cover if we go deeper into probabilistic model selection — conceptually playing the same role as Elbow/Silhouette did for K-Means).
19 · everything in one page

Class 04: the complete picture

1

Hard clustering forces certainty

K-Means and Hierarchical both give exactly one cluster per point — GMM instead gives a genuine probability distribution over ALL clusters.

2

A Gaussian needs only μ and σ (or Σ)

Mean controls position, variance/covariance controls shape — this holds identically from 1D through N-D.

3

π breaks ties that density alone can't

A rare-but-good-fit Gaussian should NOT beat a common-and-decent-fit Gaussian — π (mixture weight) is what encodes that.

4

EM alternates 2 simple steps

E-step: compute soft responsibilities. M-step: recompute μ, Σ, π as responsibility-weighted averages. Repeat to convergence.

5

Every formula generalizes cleanly

1D → 2D → N-D → K clusters all use the SAME formulas — scalars simply become vectors/matrices, and a fixed "2" becomes a general "K."

6

Responsibility is the whole idea

γ_ik — "how much does Gaussian k explain THIS point" — is computed for every point, every Gaussian, every iteration. Nothing else in GMM is more central than this one number.

K-Means / HierarchicalGMM
MembershipHard — exactly one clusterSoft — probability across all clusters
Cluster shapeSpherical (K-Means) or linkage-dependentElliptical — captures correlation between features
What it outputsA labelA full probability distribution + a label (if you want one)
Fitting mechanismIterative reassignment / mergingExpectation-Maximization (E-step / M-step)

The one-sentence mental model

K-Means asks "which centroid is closest?" and forces an answer. GMM asks "how well does each of these K bell-curves explain this exact point?" and is honest when the answer is "a bit of both."
Coming up in the next class: everything today was the math and the manual computation, by design — no code, no shortcuts. Next class picks up exactly here and goes deep on the CODE side: fitting GMM with sklearn.mixture.GaussianMixture, reading out predict_proba() for the full soft responsibility matrix, and — critically — exactly how GMM converts those soft responsibilities into a single hard label when you call .predict() (spoiler: it's the argmax of γ, but we'll unpack why that's a legitimate simplification and when it can mislead you). We'll also cover initialization in practice using init_params='kmeans' vs 'random', and how convergence is actually detected (log-likelihood plateauing, not just "parameters stop moving").
